question: What does CanIPlay measure?
quick: CanIPlay uses browser HTTP and image probes to estimate endpoint timing and reachability; it does not directly measure ICMP ping or a game session’s network path.
standard:
CanIPlay is a browser-based tool for estimating endpoint reachability and timing as a guide to connection quality. Its main value is making a few network observations easy to inspect in the browser. The important qualification is that it measures browser-level HTTP or image-probe behavior; it is not an ICMP ping utility and it does not directly test the UDP traffic used by many games.

The inspected code has a fetch-based probe using no-cors mode and an image-loading probe. It measures elapsed time with performance.now. That interval can include DNS resolution, connection setup, TLS negotiation, server behavior, caching, and browser policy, depending on the endpoint and connection state. Consequently, the displayed time is not a pure measurement of network round-trip latency.

The stability feature repeats probes and summarizes successful timings. It uses mean absolute deviation for its jitter value and the fraction of failed probes for a value named packetLoss. Those are useful summaries when described precisely, but failed HTTP probes are not direct measurements of lost network packets. The code also treats certain fast failures as reachable, which can confuse a quick rejection with a successful connection.

I would explain the project through that measurement boundary: it offers browser observations that can help compare endpoints or repeated runs, but cannot guarantee that a game session will be playable. A stronger version would expose an inconclusive result, retain raw samples, and clearly distinguish success, rejection, and timeout. Controlled endpoints would let those interpretations be tested before making stronger reliability claims.

A stronger version would expose an inconclusive result, retain raw samples, and clearly distinguish success, rejection, and timeout. There is also a useful concurrency discussion in the implementation. Server tests run in batches of four, which limits simultaneous work, but canceling the outer run does not directly abort every in-flight fetch because probes create separate controllers. A proposed fix would link cancellation signals and assign each run an identifier so delayed results from an old run cannot overwrite a new one.

For validation, I would use endpoints with known delays and failures, run with both cold and warm connections, and record sample counts. Comparison with a separate network tool can reveal disagreement, but the tools measure different paths and protocols. I would avoid presenting that disagreement as proof that one measurement is necessarily wrong.
mistake: Calling browser fetch timing game-server ping.

question: How are jitter and packet loss calculated?
quick: The stability test averages successful timings, uses mean absolute deviation for jitter and failed probes for a failure percentage.
standard:
The stability test averages successful timings, uses mean absolute deviation for jitter and failed probes for a failure percentage.

runStabilityTest runs multiple probes with delays. It computes the mean, min and max of reachable timings. The variable packetLoss is one minus the successful-probe fraction, and jitter is the average absolute deviation from the mean.

For a simple illustration, successful timings of 40, 50, and 60 milliseconds have a mean of 50 and a mean absolute deviation of about 6.7 milliseconds. That statistic describes spread in the observed timings. It is not the same as standard deviation or a protocol-specific jitter estimator. If one of four probes fails, the failure fraction is 25%, but that does not tell us which network packets were lost.

These definitions matter because familiar labels can make a browser heuristic sound more precise than it is. I would show the sample count and raw results alongside the summary.

Those names should be qualified: HTTP probe failure rate is not measured network packet loss. Results also inherit the fast-error reachability heuristic. Report sample count and uncertainty; a handful of successes cannot prove a stable low-latency connection.

question: How does cancellation interact with concurrency?
quick: testAllServers runs batches of four, while cancel marks the outer controller aborted.
standard:
testAllServers runs batches of four, while cancel marks the outer controller aborted.

The loop checks the outer signal before new probes and between batches. Each fetch creates its own AbortController. Canceling the outer controller therefore does not directly abort every in-flight request. A new run can overlap with old work if state is reset early.

Batching controls how much work is launched at once, while cancellation controls whether existing work should continue. They solve different problems. In this implementation, checking the outer signal can prevent the next batch from starting, but it does not automatically stop a request whose inner controller is unrelated.

The visible bug risk appears when a user cancels and immediately restarts. An old probe can finish later and update results belonging to the new run. I would use a run identifier as well as linked cancellation so stale completions are ignored even when a request cannot be interrupted immediately.

I would pass a shared cancellation signal into probes or link child controllers, use a run ID to ignore stale results and clean timers in finally. Test cancellation mid-batch, an immediate restart and delayed responses arriving after cancellation. These are proposed fixes to explain from the inspected code.

quick: I need to connect my own contribution to specific files, commits and decisions before giving this answer.
standard:
I need to connect my own contribution to specific files, commits and decisions before giving this answer.

Use the source links to identify the execution path, then name the part you owned and what changed. Repository ownership alone does not establish sole authorship, the hardest bug, a team disagreement or the outcome of an experiment.

A contribution story for this project should name a real user-facing problem and the code that addressed it. Possible areas include probe interpretation, result presentation, bounded concurrency, or stale updates after cancellation. The source makes those areas available for discussion, but it does not establish which one I personally designed or fixed.

Once ownership is confirmed, I would explain the original behavior, a reproducible example, the chosen change, and its limitation. A precise statement about improving cancellation correctness is more defensible than an unsupported claim that the tool accurately predicts every game's network performance.

question: How would you make CanIPlay’s measurements reproducible?
quick: Use controlled endpoints, record raw samples and disclose what each timing includes.
standard:
Use controlled endpoints, record raw samples and disclose what each timing includes.

The existing history keeps a bounded set of recent results and the probe count is configurable. Results vary with cache, DNS, TLS, browser policy and endpoint behavior. Repeat measurements and compare distributions rather than a single number.

Reproducibility starts by recording what was measured. I would keep the endpoint, timestamp, browser conditions, and individual probe outcomes, then summarize the distribution. A warm connection can avoid setup work that appears in a cold run, so comparing one cold observation with one warm observation can lead to the wrong conclusion about the network.

Controlled test endpoints would deliberately respond quickly, respond after a delay, fail, or time out. That gives the tool known situations against which to check its status labels and elapsed-time calculations.

Add run IDs, browser/network metadata and a distinction between successful response, fast failure and timeout. Cross-check against a trusted network tool on the same host without pretending the two measurements are identical. Benchmarks should retain the actual endpoint and timestamp.
